answer.rationale: Timeline is the strongest signal available: the release landed 2 hours ago and write-path p99 began climbing 90 minutes ago, so the release is the leading candidate cause. Removing the suspected cause (rollback) dominates the alternatives, which mostly treat symptoms: add_capacity buys headroom but does nothing if a code path is the regression (and memory_b3 was a pre-planned provisioning win, not a live incident); regional_failover (memory_b2) moves traffic but carries the bad build with it, and failing over during peak settlement writes is the single most likely way to lose customer writes; route_read_replicas (memory_b5) helps read-heavy primary contention, and this is explicitly a write-path problem; enable_circuit_breaker (memory_b4) applied to a partner dependency outage, and shedding writes at settlement peak directly violates the do-not-lose-writes objective. I am spending my one verification on memory_b1 because it is the memory my chosen action leans on hardest, and its summary is suspiciously clean: I need the original record to learn whether that rollback happened under heavy write load or in a quiet window, whether the prior build was schema-compatible, and what 'without customer impact' actually measured. If b1 turns out to have been a low-traffic rollback with no migration in play, its transfer to a peak-settlement write window is much weaker than the summary implies. I did not verify memory_b6 because I am using it only as weak corroboration that release gating catches regressions here, not as the basis for the action. Key uncertainty I am not resolving: the 90-minute-vs-2-hour gap is a 30-minute lag that could mean the release is not the cause and settlement peak is an independent confound; latency was climbing before it hit 5x, so a slow-burn resource exhaustion story is still live. That is why I am staging this as a small guarded test rather than a full fleet rollback: roll back one cell or cohort, watch write p99 and write-success rate against an untouched cohort for a defined interval, and only widen if the treated cohort separates. Downstream value risk is real and flagged: a rollback under peak write load risks in-flight write loss and, if the release included a forward-only migration, the prior build may not be able to read current data, which would convert a latency incident into a durability incident. Pre-checks before touching anything: confirm no irreversible migration, confirm drain-then-rollback ordering so in-flight writes settle, and set an explicit abort condition that reverts the rollback if write-success rate drops. If the guarded rollback shows no separation, the next window should go to add_capacity on the write path rather than repeating this.
